Device Simulation of CsPbBr3 Solar Cells for
High-Efﬁciency Blue Light Photovoltaic Power Converters
Yuejie Tan and Shinsuke Miyajima*
1. Introduction
The development of wireless power transfer (WPT) systems has
attracted signiﬁcant attention, especially for battery charging
of electric vehicles, implantable medical devices, etc.[1,2] Home
applications such as controllers and smartphones have been
commercialized as being capable of wireless charging. However,
the main challenges of current WPT systems are the short power-
transmission distance and electromagnetic interference,[3] which
affect electromagnetic noise to electrical devices and the human
body.[4] To solve the problem of short-distance transmission,
there are two options: the WPT technique using microwaves
or the optical wireless power transfer (OWPT) technique using
light. Both techniques have the potential for long-distance power
transmission. OWPT has several advantages over microwave
WPT in some respects. These advantages include small equip-
ment size, no electromagnetic noise, and the possibility of
underwater applications. Therefore, we
focus on OWPT in this study.
As a WPT technique, OWPT has a high
potential to deliver watt-level power over a
meter-level distance without electromag-
netic interference. As shown in Figure 1a,
a monochromatic light source, laser, or
light-emitting diode (LED) is used as the
light source to convert electric power into
light, which passes through the transmis-
sion medium, and ﬁnally, the solar cell con-
verts the light into electricity, which can be
supplied to a wide range of applications,
from charging implantable medical devices
through the human skin[4] to sending
power through water.[5,6] The solar cell in
the OWPT system is referred to as a pho-
tovoltaic power converter. The efﬁciency
of the OWPT system is determined by
the product of three efﬁciencies: light source, transmission,
and photovoltaic power converter. For relatively short distances,
up to 10 m in air, the effect of light source beam absorption and
scattering by air can be almost neglected. Therefore, high trans-
mission efﬁciency is expected if the light beam can be adjusted to
the photovoltaic power converter by applying appropriate object
detection techniques using sensors.[7,8] In underwater applica-
tions, the absorption loss due to water is greater than that due
to air. However, it is still signiﬁcantly lower than that due to
microwave or radio frequency, which demonstrates the superior-
ity of this system. It can be concluded that the efﬁciency of the
OWPT system is primarily determined by the conversion efﬁ-
ciencies of the light source and photovoltaic power converter,
except for extremely long-distance power transmission, such
as over 100 m.
From the perspective of light source efﬁciency, there are not
many light source wavelength options. According to the litera-
ture, various semiconductor lasers,[9,10] including edge laser
diode (LDs), vertical cavity surface emitting lasers (VCSELs),
and LEDs, can achieve high conversion efﬁciency exceeding
50%. Speciﬁcally, near-infrared lasers perform optimally in
the 800–1000-nm wavelength range,[9,11,12] whereas blue lasers
are most efﬁcient at ≈450 nm.[13–17] For near-infrared lasers, a
VCSEL light source can achieve wall plug efﬁciency (WPE)
exceeding 63%,[18] whereas edge LDs have demonstrated
remarkable efﬁciency of up to 85% at 50 °C and 76% at
10 °C.[11] Previous studies also indicate that blue LEDs can
achieve WPE of above 49.1%,[15] with notable cases reaching
over 70% for III-nitride LEDs emitting at 455 nm.[17] In 2010,
a LED with efﬁciency of 85.9% at a wavelength of 444 nm
was achieved by optimizing the epitaxial structure, growth

The performance of CsPbBr3 solar cells is investigated using device simulation
to clarify the criteria for obtaining high-efﬁciency blue light photovoltaic power
converters. The results show that the conduction band offset between the
electron transport layer (ETL) and CsPbBr3 layer signiﬁcantly impacts conversion
efﬁciency. The best device performance is obtained when the conduction band of
the ETL is 0.4 eV higher than that of the CsPbBr3 layer. Simulations also revealed
that gallium nitride is preferred to conventional titanium oxide (TiO2) as the ETL
material. The analysis indicates that the carrier diffusion length of the CsPbBr3
layer signiﬁcantly affects the short-circuit current density and ﬁll factor of devices
and that a carrier diffusion length of at least 0.5 μm is required to realize high-
efﬁciency devices. The use of a transparent conductive oxide layer with a work
function smaller than 4.0 eV or the insertion of a buffer layer with electron afﬁnity
less than 4.1 eV can effectively improve the open-circuit voltage of devices.

light is considered one of the optimum light sources for high-
efﬁciency OWPT.
In the case of photovoltaic power converters, high-efﬁciency
devices have only been developed for near-infrared light.[19]
GaAs photovoltaic power converters have exhibited conversion
efﬁciency of 68.9% for 858 nm monochromatic light with a
light intensity of 11.4 W cm2 (about 60% for 0.1 W cm2).[20]
Although high-efﬁciency photovoltaic power converters for blue
light sources have not yet been developed, a promising material
choice is CsPbBr3 (a bandgap of 2.3 eV).[21] This material has a
bandgap energy comparable to the photon energy of blue light
(2.7 eV). It also exhibits greater stability against moisture and
oxygen than other halide perovskite materials.[22–24] CsPbBr3
is primarily investigated as a light-absorbing material for multi-
junction solar cells. Theoretical work has demonstrated the
potential of this material for use as the light-absorbing material
of power converters in OWPT systems.[23] A recently reported
CsPbBr3 solar cell exhibited conversion efﬁciency of 10.79%
under AM1.5G and 100 mW cm2 illumination (sunlight)[25]
and estimated conversion efﬁciency of ≈43.5% under a blue light
source (estimated from solar cell performance under AM1.5G
illumination and external quantum efﬁciency [EQE]). Our group
has also developed a CsPbBr3 photovoltaic power converter;
however, its conversion efﬁciency under blue light was only
≈20%.[10,26,27] The aforementioned conversion efﬁciencies are
signiﬁcantly lower than their theoretical values. Therefore, it
is important to analyze the efﬁciency- limiting factor and the
quality of the CsPbBr3 layer in the photovoltaic power converter.
In addition, the electron transport layer (ETL) (Figure 1a) is
essential to obtain high-efﬁciency devices. The role of the ETL
is to selectively transport electrons. For effective electron
transport, an ETL with suitable band alignment is critical. We
intensively investigated the inﬂuence of the ETL on device
performance in this study.
At present, device simulations of perovskite solar cells with
bandgaps (1.3–1.9 eV) suitable for normal solar cell application
have been intensively reported.[28–31] However, there are a few
reports on the device simulation of CsPbBr3 solar cells.[32] In
addition, device simulation of CsPbBr3 solar cells as photovoltaic
power converters has not been reported. Therefore, device
simulations of CsPbBr3 photovoltaic power converters were
performed to obtain criteria for high-efﬁciency CsPbBr3 photo-
voltaic power converters in this study. The effect of conduction
band offset between the ETL and the CsPbBr3 layer was investi-
gated. The results highlight the suitable ETL material choice for
devices using CsPbBr3 as the light-absorbing layer. Speciﬁcally,
the interface between the ETL and CsPbBr3 layer, the quality of
the CsPbBr3 layer, and the interface between the ETL and trans-
parent conductive oxide (TCO) layer were also investigated.
2. Simulation Details
We used a one-dimensional device simulator (AFORS-HET)[33]
in our device simulation. As shown in Figure 1a,b, the structure
of the simulated-CsPbBr3 photovoltaic power converter is glass/
TCO layer/ETL/front interface layer (FIL)/CsPbBr3 layer/rear
interface layer (RIL)/hole transport layer (HTL)/Au. Spiro
OMETAD was adopted as the HTL, and two interface layers
(FIL and RIL) were introduced to consider carrier recombination
at the interface of the two layers. The electrical and optical param-
eters of the interface layers were consistent with those of the
CsPbBr3 layer. As shown in Figure 1b, the structure of the
CsPbBr3 photovoltaic power converter adopts a perovskite solar
cell structure with an n-i-p conﬁguration.[34] The electrical param-
eters used in the simulations are summarized in Table 1. These
parameters are obtained from previous studies.[35–37] The surface
reﬂectance of the device was calculated separately using e-ARC[38]
and was implemented in the calculation using AFORS-HET.

The thickness of the CsPbBr3 layer is also important because it
affects light absorption and photogenerated carrier collection. The
thicker the CsPbBr3 layer, the greater the light absorption. In con-

and CsPbBr3 layer on device performance when ﬂuorine-doped
tin oxide (FTO, work function of 4.4 eV)[41] was used as the TCO
layer material was investigated. Similar to the ΔEc between the
ETL and CsPbBr3 layer, it is also important to consider the band
alignment between the TCO layer and the ETL. Therefore, we
investigated the effect of the TCO work function on device per-
formance. In these simulations, we used nc-GaN as the ETL
material and the TCO work function was varied from 3.9 to

4. Conclusion
Device simulations of CsPbBr3 photovoltaic power converters
were performed to identify the criteria for obtaining high-
efﬁciency devices. The simulation results highlighted that the
conduction band offset at the ETL/CsPbBr3 layer interface signif-
icantly affected the device performance. The best conduction
band offset was 0.4 eV, which appeared as a spike structure,
and a larger conduction band offset degraded device perfor-
mance. The simulation results also highlight that TiO2, a conven-
tional ETL material for standard perovskite solar cells, is not
suitable for CsPbBr3 photovoltaic power converters. We pro-
posed and demonstrated the potential of nanocrystalline GaN
ETLs using device simulations. The effect of the quality of the
CsPbBr3 layer was also investigated. According to the results,
the carrier diffusion length primarily determines Jsc and FF;
however, the defect density is the limiting factor of Voc. The effect
of the TCO layer/ETL interface was also investigated. The band
alignment of this interface also affects device performance. Our
simulation revealed that the use of a low TCO work function or
the insertion of a buffer layer with small electron afﬁnity can mit-
igate the problem of the TCO layer/ETL interface. Finally, we
analyzed our experimentally obtained device using our developed
simulation model. By adjusting the interface defect density and
the quality of the CsPbBr3 layer, we successfully reproduced the
J–V curves and EQE results. This indicates the reliability of our
simulation model. Using this model, we also discussed ways to
improve device performance.
